title: Sell Mineral Rights in Reeves County, TX/NM
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Reeves County, TX | Delaware Basin
metaDescription: Reeves County sits in the busiest part of the Delaware Basin. If you own minerals or royalty near Pecos or Toyah, get a real number based on current activity.
heroLead: Reeves County, with Pecos as the county seat, is about as active as Permian drilling gets right now, and that activity is exactly what's pushing offers on private minerals here higher than in quieter counties.
intro: I've driven the roads around Pecos and Toyah enough times to lose count of the frac spreads, water lines, and man-camp trailers that have gone up in the last several years. This is stacked-pay country — Wolfcamp, Bone Spring, and Avalon shale all producing from the same general acreage, sometimes from the same multi-well pad drilled to different depths. That kind of density is exactly why Reeves County minerals tend to command real attention from buyers.

But density also means complexity. A single section here might have three or four operators with overlapping units at different depths, produced water recycling infrastructure crossing the surface, and permits stacking up faster than most owners can track on their own. If you've got a royalty check coming out of Reeves County, or a mineral deed your family's held since before any of this started, I'll walk you through exactly what's producing under your acres before quoting anything.

sections.heading: Pecos, Toyah, and the busiest stretch of the Delaware Basin
paragraphs: Pecos sits close to the center of the most heavily drilled part of the Delaware Basin, and the pace of permitting here over the last decade has been hard to match anywhere else in the play. Toyah, a little east along the old Texas and Pacific rail line, sits in similarly active acreage. If your family's minerals are anywhere in this corridor, there's a good chance multiple operators have looked at your section even if only one currently holds the lease.

That density cuts both ways for owners. It generally means stronger current activity and more competitive leasing, but it also means more overlapping paperwork — separate units for separate formations stacked on the same surface acres — which takes a careful hand to untangle before anyone can tell you what your specific interest is worth.

sections.heading: Stacked benches mean stacked units
paragraphs: Because Reeves County produces from multiple formations at different depths under the same acreage, it's common for your minerals to be pooled into more than one spacing unit simultaneously — one for a Wolfcamp bench, another for Bone Spring, sometimes a third. Each unit can have a different operator, different working interest partners, and a different decline curve.

That means a Reeves County owner might get two or three separate royalty checks off the same tract, each behaving differently. It's one of the more common sources of confusion I run into with owners here, and it's also why a fair valuation has to account for every unit your acreage touches, rather than only the one you happen to have a check for.

sections.heading: Water, infrastructure, and what it means for your minerals
paragraphs: The scale of drilling in Reeves County has driven massive investment in produced water recycling and disposal infrastructure — pipelines, recycling facilities, and salt water disposal wells that crisscross the county alongside the oil and gas wells themselves. None of that changes your mineral ownership directly, but it's a reasonable proxy for how committed operators are to this acreage long-term: nobody builds permanent water infrastructure on ground they plan to walk away from soon.
For owners deciding whether to hold or sell, that long-term operator commitment is worth factoring in. It generally supports continued development rather than a quick boom-and-bust.

sections.heading: Title work through the Reeves County clerk's office
paragraphs: Reeves County has seen enough oil-driven land transactions over the past century that courthouse records in Pecos can run deep and, in places, messy — assignments from decades ago, name variations across generations, and fractional interests split among heirs who've since moved away from West Texas entirely. A buyer working in good faith runs full title before closing regardless of what paperwork you personally have on hand.

If you've got a division order number, an old lease, or even just a check stub, that's enough to start. We do the courthouse work from there and tell you honestly if anything needs to be cleared before we can close.

faqs.question: Why does my Reeves County royalty check come from a different operator than the one I originally leased with?
faqs.answer: Leases and operating rights change hands frequently in an active area like this. Operators buy, sell, and swap acreage regularly, and your division order should reflect the current operator. If your paperwork looks outdated, we can help track down who's currently paying and what unit you're in.

faqs.question: I get two separate royalty checks for what I thought was one piece of land. Is that normal?
faqs.answer: Very common in Reeves County. Because multiple formations are developed at different depths under the same surface acreage, your minerals can be pooled into separate units for each bench, each paying its own royalty. We account for every unit your tract touches when we value your interest.

faqs.question: Is Reeves County still seeing new wells, or has development slowed?
faqs.answer: It remains one of the more actively permitted counties in the Delaware Basin. That said, activity varies block by block, so we check current permitting near your specific unit rather than assuming based on the county's overall reputation.

faqs.question: Does the water recycling and pipeline infrastructure on the surface affect my mineral value?
faqs.answer: Not directly — that's surface infrastructure and doesn't change your mineral ownership. But it's a reasonable signal that operators are committed to developing this acreage for the long haul, which we factor into how we think about future activity on your tract.

faqs.question: How fast can you close on a Reeves County mineral sale?
faqs.answer: With clean, traceable title we can often close in two to four weeks. Given how much land here has changed hands over the decades, some tracts need extra title work first — we'll tell you honestly which situation yours is before you sign anything.
